title: Deer antler trophic memory is a rewritable pattern memory

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Deer antler trophic memory is a rewritable pattern memory

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In deer, a wound made on a branched antler in one year leads to ectopic tines at the same location in later years after the antler is shed, which the author interprets as an experience-dependent, rewritable pattern memory in which the target morphology is rewritten without changing the genome.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Levin M 2022, Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds › Somatic Cognition: An Example of Unconventional Agency in Detail › Pattern Memory: A Key Component of Homeostatic Loops

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: This is an example of experience-dependent, re-writable pattern memory, in which the target morphology (the setpoint for anatomical homeostasis) is re-written within standard hardware.

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Levin M, “Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds”, Frontiers in systems neuroscience (2022), doi:10.3389/fnsys.2022.768201; section “Somatic Cognition: An Example of Unconventional Agency in Detail › Pattern Memory: A Key Component of Homeostatic Loops”. Scope: Antlered deer (Cervidae) after antler injury

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2022-tame-13: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.42

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Spatial recurrence across antler cycles is observable, but public data are limited and likely heterogeneous. Existing cases can support persistence, not uniquely resolve the proposed memory framing.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use longitudinal antler records to compare later ectopic tine location with prior wound location, controlling antler identity and normal branching variation; persistence after shedding would support a lasting local state.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Evidence appears to be sparse case records rather than an open cohort.

Local scarring or altered stem-cell niches are rival mechanisms.

Pattern memory is an interpretation of persistent local effects.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.38
operationalizability: 0.62
discriminating power: 0.4
analysis feasibility: 0.48
data adequacy: 0.25

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Location-specific ectopic tines in later antler cycles are described in published case literature and could be compiled for a weak spatial test. There is no public table of wound coordinates, subsequent tines, and controls. Scar and structural damage remain competing accounts, so existing reports can illustrate the pattern and cannot settle the memory interpretation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Pair the location of an antler wound in one year with tine positions after shedding, against unwounded antlers; a rewritable target holds if ectopic tines recur at the wound site and can be changed by a later injury.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Local scar, pedicle damage, or broken bone can place a tine without a rewritten morphological setpoint.

Few species and few animals are described quantitatively.

The observations are case reports and older natural-history figures, not a coordinate database.
